explanation: BCNF requires every determinant to be a candidate key. In this relation, Advisor -> Course holds, but Advisor alone is not a candidate key, so BCNF is violated. The relation can still satisfy 3NF because Course is a prime attribute: it is part of the candidate key (Student, Course). That makes option A the best description of the BCNF-specific problem.

options.text: A determinant is not a candidate key.
A nonkey attribute depends transitively on the key.
A nonkey attribute depends on only part of a composite key.

prompt: Consider a relation R(Student, Course, Advisor) with functional dependencies {Student, Course} -> Advisor and Advisor -> Course. Assume the candidate keys are (Student, Course) and (Student, Advisor). Which issue shows that R can be in third normal form but still violate BCNF?
reviewConcept: BCNF identifies cases where a nonkey determinant remains in the relation.
